title: A party card game where [[one number]] runs every turn
hook: 5 Dead is a web card game I designed and built on my own. You can play against bots, pass one phone round a table of up to 24 people, or open an online room. Every turn comes down to keeping a shared total at 21 or under.

facts.label: For
facts.value: Friends and families playing together, 2 to 24 players

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Web app you can install. Plays offline. Phones play held sideways

facts.label: Stack
facts.value: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers, D1 with Drizzle, Tailwind CSS 4

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Playable. Not yet tested with groups of players

summary: The problem: a card table has to show several things at once, the total, whose turn it is, what a card does and who is still alive, on screens as small as a phone held sideways.
What I built: an installable web game with bots, pass and play on one device, and online rooms, all running the same rules engine.
The key idea: put the running total in the middle and keep choosing a card separate from playing it. The throw gesture took three rounds to get right while the rules stayed strict.
Where it stands: playable, with 29 automated tests. Friends played it at a game night. Beyond that I have no usage numbers.

lead.alt: The 5 Dead game table on a computer: an oval table with the running total 5 in the middle, three opponents around it and a fanned hand of ten cards along the bottom
lead.caption: A pass and play game on a computer. The total is 5, it is your turn, and your hand is sorted from high to low. The backdrop, the character portraits and the card back are painted out in flat colour: they are generated pictures, not my design.

sections.label: Why I built it
sections.heading: A card game the whole table can follow, on whatever devices are in the room

blocks.p: 5 Alive is a printed card game. Players take turns adding cards to one shared total. Go past 21 and you lose a life. Action cards reset the total, skip players or make everyone else draw.

I wanted a version friends and families could play together on phones, tablets and computers, with or without a network. 5 Dead is my own independent game built on those rules. It is not made with or approved by Hasbro, which publishes 5 Alive. There was no client: the brief was my own.

figures.alt: Diagram of a number line from 0 to 21 with 16 highlighted, above four groups of cards: add to the total, set the total, hit everyone else and change the table
figures.caption: The whole game in one picture. At 16, a 5 is the highest number card that keeps you safe. The pink boxes are the two ways lives are lost.

blocks.p: The hard part is the screen. At any moment a player needs the total, whose turn it is, what the card they are holding will do and who is still in. With up to 24 players, that has to fit on a phone held sideways.

aside.title: What I do not have.
aside.detail: Apart from that game night with friends I have not run play sessions, and I have no usage numbers. Nothing on this page reports what players said or did.

sections.label: How it works
sections.heading: Pick who is at the table, then play

blocks.p: The setup asks one question first: who is at the table? The answer decides how many devices you need and whether you need a network.

figures.alt: Diagram comparing three modes, Bots, Pass and play, and Online room, by players, devices, network, hidden hands and what happens if you leave
figures.caption: The three modes side by side. Read the Network row: only the online room needs a connection after the first load.

figures.alt: The phone setup screen with tabs for Bots, Pass and play, and Online, a name field, a player counter set to 4 and a Let's play button
figures.caption: Setup on a phone. One short form. The line under the button says what this mode needs: no Wi-Fi.

figures.alt: The How to play guide on a phone listing special cards such as Skip, Set to 21, Reset, Reshuffle and Bomb, each with a one-line explanation
figures.caption: The rules guide. It uses the same card faces as the game, so a card looks the same here and in your hand.

blocks.p: In pass and play, one device goes round the table. Between turns a cover screen hides the last hand and names the next player. Nobody sees cards until that player taps to reveal them.

figures.alt: The table with a cover panel across the bottom reading Pass to Player 3 and a Show my cards button
figures.caption: The cover screen between turns. The hand area is replaced by one instruction and one button. The backdrop, the character portraits and the card back are painted out in flat colour: they are generated pictures, not my design.

sections.label: Decision 1
sections.heading: The total sits in the middle, and everything else sits around it

blocks.p: What you see: the running total is the largest thing on the screen. The real last card sits beside it. Opponents sit around the table and your hand runs along the bottom.

figures.alt: The computer table with eight numbered notes: the total, the play pile, the direction of play, the turn cue, the mode label, a seat's lives and card count, the sorted hand and the Play button
figures.caption: Start with notes 1 and 3: the total and the direction of play sit together, because a Reverse changes both what happens next and who acts.

blocks.p: In the build: my first release was a quiet, flat table on a charcoal page, with soft yellow, teal and lilac cards. Twenty minutes later I replaced it. The new table is laid out like mobile card games such as UNO Mobile: a landscape table, big overlapping cards and clear feedback when an action lands. The rules did not change, and the identity and card faces stay my own.

figures.alt: The first release's home page: a large headline reading Five lives, zero mercy, a fan of pastel cards and the start of the setup panel
figures.caption: The first release's home page, from the same morning. The pastel card faces were later replaced.

blocks.p: Your hand is sorted from 7 down to 0, then action cards in a fixed order. Sorting only changes what you see. A test checks that it never changes the actual deal. At exactly 21 the total changes colour and reads "On the edge".

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: Every action now plays an effect across the table: a bomb sends out a shockwave, a reverse sweeps round. Effects can hide whose turn it is. So effects play one at a time from a queue, bots wait for the current one to finish, and the reduced-motion setting drops the movement but keeps the text and colour cues.

aside.title: About the screens on this page.
aside.detail: The game has a painted night-sky backdrop, six character portraits and an illustrated card back. They are generated pictures, not my design work, so I have painted them out of every screen here. Everything else is the real interface.

sections.label: Decision 2
sections.heading: Choosing a card is not the same as playing it

blocks.p: What you see: one tap lifts a card and ticks it. Nothing is played yet. The Play button then commits it, and the line under the button says what the card will do.

figures.alt: A hand of ten cards with the yellow 7 lifted and ticked, and a Play button on the right with the line Add this number to the total
figures.caption: A selected card. Look under Play: "Add this number to the total." The hint changes with the card you hold.

blocks.p: For people who know the game there are faster ways: double-tap a card, toss it upward, or drop it anywhere on the table.

figures.alt: Diagram of how far a finger must move upward before a card lifts or plays, with a list of gestures and what each one does
figures.caption: The gesture rules. Small movements never play a card. Each pink row on the right is a way to back out.

blocks.p: In the build: getting the toss right took three rounds on the same morning. Each round added tests that describe the gesture in plain words.

steps.title: Round 1
steps.detail: Drag a card onto the table, or throw it there. Sideways swipes, slow releases, short twitches and throws away from the table never play a card.

steps.title: Round 2
steps.detail: A slow drop on the table's rim also plays. So does a card held by its corner, once your grip reaches the table.

steps.title: Round 3
steps.detail: A small upward toss plays before the card reaches the table, with no speed or aim needed. Taps, flat swipes on a long hand and downward drags stay in the hand.

blocks.p: A shared guard stops a card from being played twice by a double click straight after a drag. The pointer maths also accounts for the rotated phone layout described below.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: Select then Play costs an extra tap for experienced players. I kept it as the main path because it is the one that works for everyone, including keyboard users, and made the shortcuts forgiving instead.

sections.label: Decision 3
sections.heading: The card face tells you what the card does

blocks.p: What you see: number cards and action cards look different at a glance. Each kind of action has its own colour, symbol and short label.

figures.alt: Before and after strips of the same phone hand: pastel cards with a ring on every face, then bold cards with a coloured corner, a black field and a label strip on action cards
figures.caption: Two hands from the same phone layout, 17 minutes apart. In the after strip, find the Reshuffle card on the right: magenta, its own symbol, its own label.

blocks.p: In the build: every face is one component drawn in code, not an image. Each face measures its own width, so the corner number, the centre mark and the label scale with the card, not with the size of the hand. Number cards repeat their number in the opposite corner. Action cards drop that second number so it can never collide with the label.

The colours follow the cues of the printed game: blue and cyan for draw cards, lime for reset, magenta for reshuffle and pass, orange for reverse. The Bomb has a charcoal and red face inside a gold frame, with a fuse blast. The Reshuffle shows cards inside circular arrows.

figures.alt: The phone table with ten bold cards in a fan, the Reshuffle card lifted and ticked, and the Play button explaining Shuffle and re-deal all active hands, reset to zero
figures.caption: The new faces on a phone. The selected Reshuffle card is explained under Play before you commit it. The backdrop, the character portraits and the card back are painted out in flat colour: they are generated pictures, not my design.

blocks.p: Two tests guard this. One checks that every special card uses its colour and a short label that no other card shares. The other checks that the Bomb and the Reshuffle appear exactly once in every deck, at every table size.

aside.title: What I ruled out.
aside.detail: Colour alone. Borrowing the printed game's colours makes the cards familiar to people who know it, but colour cannot carry the meaning by itself, so every action card also has its own symbol and a word.

sections.label: Decision 4
sections.heading: Phones play sideways, and any hand size fits

blocks.p: What you see: on a phone the table always runs sideways. Far seats shrink to a name, hearts and a card count. When a hand gets too long for one fan, it becomes two full rows.

figures.alt: A phone table with a 24-card hand in two rows and six numbered notes on the header, the direction label, the player list, the compact far seats, the two-row hand and the Play button
figures.caption: Note 5 is the point: 24 cards, every one whole and tappable, without shrinking the controls. The backdrop, the character portraits and the card back are painted out in flat colour: they are generated pictures, not my design.

blocks.p: In the build: when a game starts on a touch device, it asks for full screen and a sideways lock. Support varies, especially on iPhones. Then the page itself rotates the live table, and the same measurements drive both versions.

list: Touch targets: 48px icon buttons, 52 to 56px main buttons and fields, and 16px text in forms.
Cards in a sideways hand stay 80 to 98px wide, with at least 52px of each card showing.
As the hand grows, the fan tightens, then splits into two rows of cards at least 44px wide. Very large hands scroll sideways, with a hint.
The space above and below the cards is reserved, so a lifted card, its outline and its tick never get cut off.

blocks.p: Two tests check that every card stays selectable inside the hand area as the count changes, on phone and computer sizes, and that the hand grows back after cards are played. I checked layouts in the browser at 320, 384 and 412px wide upright, and at 915 by 412 and 915 by 320 sideways.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: All of this was checked in a desktop browser imitating phones. Real orientation locking, notches and the Samsung browser still need testing on real devices.

sections.label: The build
sections.heading: One rules engine, used by every mode

blocks.p: The same rules engine deals, checks and applies every move. Bots and pass and play run it on the device. Online rooms run it on the server, which is the only judge of a move.

figures.alt: Diagram in three columns: on each device the screens, rules engine and offline store; online the room service and a database row per room; and what each player receives: their own hand, the public table and recent receipts
figures.caption: How it fits together. The receipts on the right let every phone play the same animation without learning anyone's private cards.

head: Part
What I used
rows: D1 (SQLite) through Drizzle, one row per room with a revision number
A service worker, with saved games in browser storage
Tailwind CSS 4, plus my own styles for the table and the cards
Made in the browser with the Web Audio API, after the first tap, with a remembered mute
29 tests run with Node's own test runner, plus a room test against a local server

blocks.p: Fairness was a rule from the start. The same deal rules and the same luck apply to every seat, bots included.

figures.alt: Diagram of four steps from secure random numbers to dealing ten cards each, with three notes on what bots, hand sorting and the online server can and cannot see
figures.caption: How a deal is made. Step 2 is the easy one to miss: without it, some cards would turn up slightly more often.

blocks.p: The printed game is for 2 to 6 players. For bigger groups I add a whole deck for every six players, so the mix of cards stays the same.

figures.alt: Bar chart of one 77-card deck: 47 number cards from 0 to 7 and 30 action cards from Reverse down to Bomb
figures.caption: One deck. Low numbers are common and the 7 is rare. The counts are my own: the published leaflet does not list them.

figures.alt: Bar chart of four table sizes, 2 to 6, 7 to 12, 13 to 18 and 19 to 24 players, each showing cards dealt and cards left to draw
figures.caption: Bigger tables. At the top of every band, 22% of the cards are left to draw from. An illustration worked out from the counts, not a measured result.

stats.label: automated tests: 16 for the rules, 13 for the interface
cards in one deck, up to four decks at once

figures.alt: Timeline of 19 October 2026 from 10:00 to midnight with nine commits, from the first release at 10:38 to the hand layout at 23:30
figures.caption: The build in one day. Most of the morning went on the throw gesture, the evening on phones and card faces.

blocks.p: The hardest problems were about trust, not looks.

head: Area
What was hard, and what I did
rows: Every phone has to animate the same draw or bomb without learning anyone else's cards. The server keeps receipts of the last 12 public actions, such as who played what and how many cards were drawn. Tests check that a receipt never reveals a private draw.

Two players can press Play at the same moment. Each room has a revision number, and a save only lands if the number has not changed since the move was checked. The losing move is rejected, not merged.
It took three rounds to make a toss feel natural without letting a twitch play a card. The tests now describe the gesture in plain sentences.
Engine tests play complete simulated games for every table size and rule variant, and check that no card is lost or created.

sections.label: Accessibility
sections.heading: Motion, sound and touch all have a quieter path

list: With reduced motion turned on, the flying cards, shockwaves and sweeps are removed. Short text and colour cues stay, so nothing important depends on movement.
Sound starts only after you tap something, the mute setting is remembered, and the game stays quiet when its tab is hidden.
Keyboard users can select a card and press Play. The drag and toss gestures are extras, never the only way.
The direction of play is shown as a word, such as Clockwise, and "Your turn" is spelled out.

aside.title: What this does not prove.
aside.detail: I have not tested the game with a screen reader, and these choices have not been checked by a disabled player.

sections.label: Where it stands
sections.heading: Playable, and not yet played by a real group

blocks.p: 5 Dead works with bots, pass and play and online rooms. Bots and pass and play keep working offline once the app has fully loaded. The code is on GitHub.
These things are not done or not known yet:

list: No group has played it. I have no player numbers, quotes or results.
Tables of seven or more follow my house rule. Tests simulate them, but no real group has tried one.
The deck counts are my own. The published leaflet explains each card but does not list how many there are.
Installing on real iPhones and Android phones has not been tested.
Old rooms stop being playable after 24 hours, but nothing yet deletes them from the database.

sections.label: What is next
sections.heading: Put it in front of a real table

list: Run a first session: start a bot game, play a special card, and see whether players can say what happens next without opening the rules.
Test the smallest phone hand and the biggest table with real people before adding more effects.
Try pass and play hand-offs and a dropped connection in an online room, and check that the bigger-table rule is clear before the game starts.
Install it on real phones, and add a clean-up job for expired rooms.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.heading: Be forgiving with input and strict with rules

blocks.p: The gesture got looser twice in one morning while the rules engine did not change at all. That split made each round cheap: the input could forgive a sloppy toss because the rules engine, not the gesture, decides what is legal.

Keeping the view apart from the deal paid off the same way. I replaced the whole table and every card face in one day, and the tests for dealing and fairness never had to move. Next time I would put the game in front of a real group before the second redesign, not after.
